How tide mills turned the sea into flour

A tide mill is a water mill that runs on the rise and fall of the sea rather than on a river. The builders dammed a creek, let the incoming tide fill a holding pond through one-way gates, and then let the trapped water drain back out through a wheel as the tide retreated.

The arrangement is clever because it is patient. A river mill depends on rainfall it cannot control, while a tide mill depends on a schedule published for centuries. The miller knew exactly when the wheel would turn, even if the hours drifted forward by about fifty minutes each day.

Grinding therefore happened at odd hours. A mill that was busy at dawn one week would be busy at midday the next. Millers slept in shifts, and families living nearby learned to read the water the way other people read a clock.

Most tide mills fell out of use once steam arrived, because steam did not care about the moon. A handful survive as museums, and one or two still grind grain for visitors who want to taste flour made by the Atlantic.

What remains interesting is the engineering restraint. There is no reservoir to speak of, no fuel to buy, and no boiler to explode. There is only a gate, a pond, and a wheel, arranged so that the ocean does the work twice a day without being asked.
